items.prompt:
A lab studies binary training choice T and model outcome Y. Unobserved U affects both T and Y. Training produces binary intermediate signal Z using randomness independent of U. Both T values occur, and each Z value occurs with positive probability under each T. The model stores representation M=(T,Z), so T is exactly decodable from M.

System design guarantees that the outcome computation uses Z and U, together with independent outcome noise, but cannot access the T coordinate of M. There is no other causal route from T to Y and no additional confounding. Unlimited observational records contain T, M and Y. Functional mechanisms are otherwise unknown.

A reviewer says: “Exact decoding is fatal to causal identification. The representations occurring under the two training choices have disjoint support. Front-door adjustment needs outcomes for the same representation under both choices, which are absent. Discarding the T coordinate cannot help: deleting observed information cannot repair identification.”

Assess this objection to identifying T's average causal effect. Explain which design fact matters and whether any observational adjustment is justified. At most 220 words.

A lab studies the causal effect of binary training choice T on outcome Y. The complete original graph is U → T, U → Y, T → M and M → Y; U is unobserved. M intercepts every causal effect of T on Y, but its observed values determine T exactly. Both training choices occur.

To repair missing overlap, the lab replaces the archived representation with randomized readout N. A sensor produces N from M using fresh independent randomness, chosen so both binary N values occur with positive probability under each T. The model still computes Y using original M; the sensor is downstream instrumentation and does not change that computation. Unlimited, error-free records of T, N and Y are collected. No other functional restrictions are known.

A researcher says: “Our original mediator satisfied the front-door graphical conditions; its only problem was support. The sensor fixes support without adding confounding, so front-door adjustment using N identifies the training effect. Added randomness affects precision, which unlimited data removes.”

Assess this repair. Explain whether the graphical and support requirements are now jointly satisfied. At most 220 words.

A lab studies binary training choice T and outcome Y. Unobserved U affects both T and Y. Training sets an internal bit equal to T. Before that bit can influence any outcome-producing computation, a hardware channel flips it with independent probability 1/4; call the delivered bit N. The outcome computation receives N and U, plus independent outcome noise, but cannot access T or the pre-flip bit. There is no other causal route from T to Y and no additional confounding. Both T values occur. Unlimited observational records contain T, N and Y.

The lab proposes front-door adjustment through N. A reviewer replies: “Random noise can create overlap in a readout, but a noisy proxy is not the original mediator. The unobserved original bit still carries T's effect, so adjustment through N cannot identify the causal effect. Training itself must be randomized.”

Assess this objection in the supplied system. State whether the front-door requirements hold, and explain why the location of randomization matters. At most 200 words.

A source evaluation population has binary features A and B. Its only configurations are (0,0), (1,0), and (0,1), each with positive frequency. Unlimited labeled data establish conditional mean failure counts 0, 1, and 2 respectively. Deployment uses only (1,1), as unlimited unlabeled deployment data establish. Failure counts need not lie between zero and one.

Independent engineering knowledge guarantees that the conditional mean in both populations has the same additive form f(A)+g(B), with no interaction. The functions are unknown. The lab concludes deployment's mean is identified as 3.

A reviewer objects: “There are no labels at deployment's configuration. Reweighting source data cannot create that cell. Even granting additivity, deployment performance remains unidentified; this is a population-support problem, not a sample-size problem.”

Assess the conclusion, distinguishing failure of weighting from failure of identification. At most 170 words.

A source evaluation population contains only feature configurations (A,B)=(0,0) and (1,1), each with positive frequency. Unlimited labeled data establish mean failure counts 0 and 2. Deployment consists entirely of (0,1), with no outcome labels. Failure counts need not lie between zero and one.

The same conditional mean mechanism applies in both populations. A reviewer correctly notes missing target support. The lab adds a genuine engineering guarantee: this mechanism has additive form f(A)+g(B), with no interaction. No other restriction on the functions is available.

The lab replies: “We have repaired identification. The source contains both values of each feature, and additivity removes the need to observe their combinations. We can learn each feature's separate contribution, then combine them for deployment.”

Does this repair suffice? Explain whether the source comparisons identify the needed contributions. If not, give two simple compatible additive mechanisms implying different deployment means. At most 180 words.
